title: Thistlefoot and the Lost Mouse
markdown:
High in the sky, fluffy clouds like spun silver, pointy peaks touching endless blue: Cloudneedle Ridge, old sighing winds and whispering pines, grand and quiet. In a cozy home carved from mountain stone lived Thistlefoot, a young ogre, skin as green as moss after spring rain, heart as big and warm as summer sun. He liked to hum rumbling tunes to the wind more than he liked to stomp and roar. Of all treasures, his most precious was not sparkly jewels but a creature so tiny it could sit on the tip of his smallest finger.

Pip, a field mouse with a brave lively spirit, fur the warm brown of fallen leaves, Thistlefoot’s best and most constant friend. A tiny spark of energy in the ogre’s peaceful mountain world. They shared quiet secrets under the soft moon and dreamed in nests of dried grass. One blustery afternoon a very loud wind howled with playful fun through the high passes. A wild gust snatched Pip right from Thistlefoot’s broad shoulder. The little mouse tumbled head over heels into the deep dark shadows of the Whispering Woods that lay like a dark cloak at the foot of their home.

Thistlefoot’s big green heart gave a sickening lurch. He looked at the thick line of trees. Voice, usually a deep rumble, shaky and high. “Pip. Oh, Pip, my little Pip, where did you go?” The old woods swallowed his cries. A cold strange feeling crept into his massive body. He could not go into the deep woods all by himself, not even for Pip. He needed help. Wisdom. A touch of mountain magic. He needed Willowisp.

With determined, slightly wobbly steps that shook the ground, he walked to the shadowy edge. Between old twisted oaks stood the funny crooked cottage of Willowisp, the wise mountain witch. Smoke smelling of dried lavender and spicy ginger curled from her moss-covered chimney. Hair white like moonlight, eyes sparkling with old knowledge. She greeted him at the door, smile as warm as a fireplace on a cold night.

“Hello, Thistlefoot. What brings you here on this windy wild day?”

He wrung enormous green hands. “Wise Willowisp. My Pip has been carried away by the wind, right into the Whispering Woods. I can’t find him. Will you help me?”

She looked at the worried ogre, starry eyes kind. “A lost friend is a heavy worry. The Whispering Woods hold many secrets, and finding the smallest creature needs a special way of seeing. I can’t go in with you; my magic is best kept close to my hearth. But I can give you a riddle. A key.” She leaned closer, eyes twinkling. “When something precious is lost, and its path is faint and very thin, look not for the big things, but for where the little things truly begin. What whispers low, and where the brightest sunbeams do not go, there you shall find what your heart longs for, I know.”

Thistlefoot furrowed his brow. “Look for the little things. Where the sunbeams don’t go.” He thanked her, a little lighter with a plan, and turned back toward the dark entrance.

At the imposing shadowy doorway two familiar figures stepped from the thick bushes. Grumbles, a badger as strong and trusty as the old rocks of Cloudneedle Ridge, fur the dark colour of rich earth. Beside him, nose twitching, Flicker, a squirrel whose movements were as quick as a thought, bright eyes missing nothing. Loyal mountain friends, always ready.

“Thistlefoot,” Grumbles rumbled, earthy and strong. “We saw you heading this way in such a hurry. What troubles you?”

Happy to see them, Thistlefoot told them about Pip and shared the riddle. Flicker, quickly on a low branch, chattered. “The little things. Where sunbeams don’t go. Shadows? The smallest beginnings. The tiniest tracks?”

Grumbles nodded, scanning the forest floor. “Whispers. Perhaps the wind left a small message. Something small barely touched the mossy stones.”

The three ventured in, one purpose. Thistlefoot, great size, careful not to step on anything delicate. Flicker, light as a feather, darted ahead, tiny quick scout. Grumbles, powerful nose, sniffed with steady dedication. They looked for the smallest almost invisible signs: a single bent blade of grass, a faint scuff on a dry leaf, a thread of spider silk on a thorny twig. They followed the deepest darkest shadows, where sunlight did not go, as Willowisp had said.

Deeper, past tall trees that seemed to whisper through their leaves. No sign of Pip. Thistlefoot’s broad shoulders hung. “Maybe it’s no use. We will never find him.”

Flicker, high in a big old fir, suddenly chirped. “Wait. Down here. I smell something wonderfully sweet. Look.” Under the thick roof of leaves, only slivers of light, a small bunch of tiny glowing flowers, soft luminous light. Moon-petal blossoms, rare, wonderfully sweet, found only in the deepest most shaded hollows. Gathered happily around them, eating a fallen glowing petal: Pip.

Thistlefoot gasped, relief so strong it made him tremble. The riddle. Pip had not been lost in danger; he had been drawn by the super sweet smell. The little things were the tiny glowing flowers. Where the sunbeams do not go: the deep shaded hollow. Pip, curious nose, had followed his senses to a secret meal.

With the gentlest most careful movements he had ever managed, Thistlefoot scooped Pip up. The mouse squeaked with happiness, nuzzling into the warm safe palm. “Oh, Pip. You gave me such a fright. But you are safe, and you have found such a lovely treat.”

They came out, Thistlefoot holding Pip, Grumbles trotting steadily, Flicker chattering on his shoulder, no longer worried. Hearts lighter as they walked back to Willowisp’s cozy cottage.

“Wise Willowisp. We found him. Drawn by the moon-petal blossoms in a deeply shaded hollow. Your riddle led us right to him.”

Willowisp smiled, old eyes twinkling. She did not add a lecture. She looked at Pip, who was already considering a nap in an ogre pocket, and at the three friends who had followed shadows instead of shouting.

As the sun began to slowly go down below the pointy mountains, painting Cloudneedle Ridge in fiery orange and warm gold, Thistlefoot, with Pip tucked safely and warmly in his pocket, walked home with Grumbles and Flicker. Their hearts were full. The Whispering Woods, once a place of scary shadows, no longer seemed so frightening. They had found a mouse at dinner, which was how you knew a riddle could be kind and a wind could be playful and a friend could still fit on the tip of a finger. Willowisp’s chimney, when they passed, still smelled of lavender and ginger, as if the hearth had been expecting them all along.
characters: Thistlefoot (young ogre who hums to the wind), Pip (a field mouse with a brave lively spirit)
